extracted.intended_audience: readers of moral/philosophical essays; educated general public interested in ethics and conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted evaluative principles and normative criteria from Montaigne's essays about virtue, conduct, learning, and treatment of animals — guidance for judging actions, character, and punishments. Focuses on what counts as virtue, how to judge deeds, and humane obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue strengthened by trial
rubrics_metrics.description: “These philosophers say that it is not enough ... to have our resolutions and our reasoning fixed above all the power of fortune, but that we are, moreover, to seek occasions wherein to put them to the proof: they would seek pain, necessity, and contempt to contend with them and to keep the soul in breath.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne endorses the idea that genuine virtue is reinforced when tested by hardship. Examples: Epaminondas refusing lawful riches to contend with poverty; Metellus resisting Saturninus; Stoic and Epicurean examples. Anti-pattern: equating absence of temptation with strong virtue; praising virtue that has never been tested as equivalent to practiced virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue refuses facility; requires difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: “Virtue refuses facility for a companion; and that the easy, smooth, and descending way ... is not that of a true virtue; she requires a rough and stormy passage.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True virtue is not the product of an easy temperament that naturally avoids vice, but of engagement with difficulty. Evaluations should value difficult, risky moral choices over effortless goodness. Example contrast: habitual habit-born innocence vs virtuous courage under danger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Death must be proportionate to life; interpret death by preceding life
rubrics_metrics.description: “Every death ought to hold proportion with the life before it; we do not become others for dying. I always interpret the death by the life preceding...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging the nobility or significance of a death, assess it in relation to the person's life and character. A dramatic or steadfast death appended to a feeble life likely indicates a feeble cause. Example: Montaigne reads Cato and Socrates' deaths in light of their lives; anti-pattern: praising a single courageous act while ignoring a life of triviality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish natural innocence from cultivated virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: “This third and last sort of virtue seems to render a man innocent, but not virtuous; free from doing ill, but not apt enough to do well: ... this condition is so near neighbour to imperfection and cowardice...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate a natural lack of temptation or an easy disposition with genuine moral worth. Cultivated virtue implies active capacity to do good under pressure; mere innocence may be near cowardice or deficient. Example: some virtues like chastity or temperance may arise from defect rather than moral strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider circumstances and whole character when judging actions
rubrics_metrics.description: “When we judge of a particular action, we are to consider the circumstances, and the whole man by whom it is performed, before we give it a name.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess actions in context (motives, situation, and the actor's general character) rather than in isolation. Montaigne warns that apparent courage can be ignorance or impulse; likewise apparent prudence may be mere fortune. Anti-pattern: attributing a fixed moral label to a single act without background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning is valuable but not equivalent to wisdom or the sovereign good
rubrics_metrics.description: “Learning is, indeed, a very great and a very material accomplishment; ... but learning yet I do not prize it at the excessive rate that some others do ... I love them well, but I do not adore them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume erudition automatically confers moral superiority. Evaluate the relation between knowledge and virtue: learning can inform virtue but is not its mother. Anti-pattern: adoring learned men or treating learning as the primary measure of moral worth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive cruelty and public torments are morally reprehensible
rubrics_metrics.description: “All that exceeds a simple death appears to me pure cruelty; especially ... to dismiss them in a good and calm condition, which cannot be, when we have agitated them by insufferable torments.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne condemns torturous punishments and public spectacles of suffering (gladiators, dismemberment). He suggests severe displays should be directed symbolically (on the dead) rather than torturing the living. Example: soldier who mutilated himself to avoid imagined torments; Roman spectacles. Policy implication: favor humane punishments; anti-pattern: celebrating cruelty as deterrence without regard for victims' souls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humane duty toward animals and plants
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is nevertheless a certain respect, a general duty of humanity, not only to beasts that have life and sense, but even to trees, and plants.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obligations of tenderness extend beyond humans: kindness, respect, and some protections are owed to animals and even plants. Montaigne cites customs (Turks' alms for beasts, Roman care of geese, burial of favored animals) as positive examples. Anti-patterns: delighting in gratuitous slaughter or enjoying spectacles of animal suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural propensions to vice can be corrected by discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: “Socrates confessed ... that it was, in truth, his natural propension, but that he had by discipline corrected it. ... Stilpo being born with addiction to wine and women, he had by study rendered himself very abstinent.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate moral character with attention to the role of self-discipline and practice: dispositions are not destiny. Praise should recognize the effort of correction. Anti-pattern: assuming innate tendencies are immutable or that no credit is due for reformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason can and should be trained to resist strong pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages on love and the chase: though pleasure may transport us, a man may sometimes, if he will, gain this point over himself ... I have experienced it in myself, and have not found Venus so imperious a goddess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne holds that appetites (including erotic desire) can be resisted by trained attention and habit; resisting is achievable, not miraculous. Use examples (contrast sudden excitement of the hunt with sexual ecstasy) to show where reason may be overwhelmed and where practice can help. Anti-pattern: treating conquest of appetite as impossible or as mere matter of luck.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not equate outward reputation or manners with inner moral conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: “I find myself in many things more under reputation by my manners than by my opinion, and my concupiscence less debauched than my reason.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between how one appears (manners, reputation) and inner principles or judgments. Moral assessment should probe inward motives and convictions rather than rely solely on outward comportment. Anti-pattern: praising someone solely for decorous behavior without examining their beliefs or impulses.
